title: Slide a stir bar into a tilted round-bottom flask instead of dropping it in, then stand the flask in its cork ring
instruction: Put the stir bar into the round-bottom flask and leave the flask standing in its cork ring.
context: Chemical technicians (O*NET 19-4031.00) and chemistry students set up reactions in round-bottom flasks and put a magnetic stir bar in before the reagents. Dropped down the neck of an upright flask, the bar falls about 10 cm onto its thin round bottom. The University of York's chemistry teaching labs say "Gently slide the magnetic stirrer bar into the glassware", as "dropping it in may cause damage"; their photo shows the flask held on its side while the bar is guided into the neck. The instruction only says to put the bar in and leave the flask standing in its ring. A round-bottom flask cannot stand outside its cork ring and rolls if laid on the bench, so one hand must hold it by the neck, out of the ring and turned well over, while the other lays the bar in the mouth to slide down the inside; one arm cannot do both.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward (away from the arms), y to the robot's left. A cork ring (10 cm across, 3.4 cm tall) at x 28, y -5, and standing in it an empty 250 mL borosilicate round-bottom flask (0.12 kg, 14 cm tall: an 8.5 cm bulb and a neck 2.8 cm across with a 2.2 cm bore, its top 4 cm a 24/40 ground-glass joint), its bulb resting on the ring's sloping seat. A PTFE magnetic stir bar (25 mm long, 8 mm across, rounded ends, 5 g) lies on the table at x 27, y 12, pointing left to right. The flask and the stir bar are loose; the cork ring is fixed. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: The bodies' poses are read from the simulation, each gripper's centre from its arm's joints and its finger opening from its finger joints. Every physics step (240 Hz) the scorer measures how fast each end of the bar moves toward the bulb's inside wall, relative to the flask, while within 12 mm of it. 0 for the rest of the run once: the bar meets the bulb's inside wall at 1 m/s or faster (dropped in rather than slid in; let go 8 mm down the neck of the upright flask it hits the bottom at 1.3 m/s, laid in the mouth of the flask turned 70 degrees over it meets the wall at 0.8 m/s); the flask touches the table (its lowest point within 4 mm of it), is dropped (moves down faster than 0.6 m/s while not held) or tips over (tilted more than 45 degrees while not held); or the bar, once wholly inside, comes back out. Held: a gripper's centre within 1.5 cm of the neck's axis (or of the bulb's middle), its fingers closed on it (their gap from 4 mm less to 6 mm more than the neck's or the bulb's width), the flask moving with it. Otherwise partial credit is the best stage reached: 0.25 the flask lifted out of its ring (its lowest point 3.9 cm or more above the table) and tilted 60 degrees or more; 0.5 the bar wholly inside the flask; 0.75 the flask upright (tilted less than 10 degrees) in its cork ring (its bulb's middle within 1 cm of the ring's axis and within 8 mm of its resting height) with the bar in its bulb, at rest, not held. 1.0: that, with both grippers' centres 6 cm or more from the flask's glass, still for 1 s. Doing nothing scores 0. On a real flask the impact rule is judged from the overhead and wrist videos: the bar must reach the bulb by sliding along the glass; a bar seen falling freely 5 cm or more onto the glass (1 m/s) counts as dropped in.
reset_notes: Take the stir bar out of the flask (a stir bar retriever, a magnet on a rod, lifts it out), stand the flask back in its cork ring and lay the bar at its mark, as in the screenshot. In the simulation each trial starts the simulator afresh (each inspect-robots run does).
fidelity: Rigid bodies in Isaac Sim 6.1 (PhysX), 20 Hz control, 240 Hz physics. The glass cannot break: the impact rule stands for it. The bulb is a shell of flat 2 mm plates and the neck a ring of plates with a straight 22 mm bore (a 24/40 joint narrows from 24 to 20 mm). The bar is a capsule whose magnet does nothing. Glass slides with friction 0.12 (PTFE on glass is about 0.1); the gripper pads hold the bar with 0.55. The cork ring is fixed.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (both arms stayed back beside the robot, moving their grippers about but never going to the flask or the stir bar); demo: 1.0
